doc.title: Sheryl Bailey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 24, 2023

title: Tunes as diary entries, naming, and the tune 'Walk Up'
summary: Her tunes are diary entries named when finished; she discusses the intervallic melody of 'Walk Up', Pat Martino's influence, bridges and instinctive form.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Does your composing necessarily reflect your mood of the day, of the time that you’re sitting down to work on something and you’re having a particularly bad spell or a good spell or a Godspell. Do you find that it comes out in your music?

Yeah, I always say, if folks see my live shows, every song, they’re more like diary entries to me, to remember places or things or more about that, stuff that was going on when I write it. So you know I might even just write the tune and then when I go to name it I — even if it takes a little time ‘til I get to that point I’ll think back of the time of the initial inspiration and the title will usually be that. So the titles are more, yes, diary entries, than anything for me.
Nice. I was listening to “Walk Up” — what kind of scales were those, do you recall?
I don’t know. They are, it’s a minor second and a major second and then it goes up a fourth and up a fourth, and up a fourth, and up a fourth.
That’s all right. I’d rather glad that it doesn’t have a particular name because I’m sure I wouldn’t know what it is.

No. Well, and it starts on — no it’s not true, anyway it’s just a melody but yes, that’s kind of an interesting tune. People like that tune a lot. And I wrote it and then I realized later, much time later, you know part of this celebration for Pat Martino was an amazing event, but anyway you know there’s a lot of discussion about, you know, and he’s a big influence on me as a guitarist but as a composer. But there was a whole thing about an exercise that he had with minor seven chords that moved down in whole steps. And it hit me, that’s where I got it, but that was something I practiced when I was a teenager, you know what I mean? So it’s just funny how things stick in your imagination and then they just sort of come out at a different time.

The tune at some point after the walking up melodies, the scales, switched into something else. And I had this feeling like — not to try and get inside your head — but you felt it was time for something else. Like okay here’s the bridge. It’s something different. How do those things occur to you?

Well I’ll tell you what, I think, I’m not, I write a lot of music but you know what? My understanding of harmony again is harmonic analysis and really learning standards and the harmonic analysis through time it just, you internalize that and you just have a natural sense of phrasing and where things should go and song form. Right? And I used to say this to anybody, whether you’re going to become a jazz player or not, just if you can get inside those songs they’re sort of a blueprint for all contemporary writing. And I think that’s what it is, that’s where it comes out. So it’s more instinctual. I don’t really write with an agenda, it just sort of, actually the ones that we play all the time with all my projects are usually the ones that kind of just flow out. So yeah you know it’s kind of natural to get to a point and go oh there’s a bridge. But I also say maybe it doesn’t need a bridge. Sometimes there are songs that don’t need a bridge.
At what point do you name them?
When they’re finished. When they’re finished. And again I’ll kind of reflect on what does this remind you of or what happened the initial — when you initially sat down and wrote it.
